text: It was three days after the search, once Tam's cellar had begun, slowly, to recover something resembling its former stock, that Will asked to speak with him privately — an unusual enough request, from a man who generally preferred an audience, that Tam set down what he was doing without argument.
Will produced a small, worn leather pouch, considerably heavier than its modest size suggested, and set it on the table between them without ceremony.

“That's the debt,” he said. “All of it, near as I can reckon the original sum plus what's fair for the waiting. I've been setting coin aside since before any of this business with Crane started — small amounts, whenever I could manage it without the others noticing. I wanted it to be mine to give you properly, not simply borrowed from a shared purse to settle an old embarrassment.”

Tam stared at the pouch for a long moment without touching it, something working across his face that took him rather longer than usual to settle into words. “You've been saving this,” he said, slowly, “since before you had any particular reason to think you'd need to make peace with me at all.”

“I've owed it a long while,” Will said, simply. “I decided, somewhere along the way, that I was tired of being a man who let debts simply age into excuses. I don't know precisely when that decision happened. I only know I kept setting coin aside afterward, and never once talked myself out of it, which is rather more discipline than I've shown about anything else in my life.”
Tam picked up the pouch, finally, weighing it in one hand with real, unhidden feeling. “Well,” he said. “I'll not pretend that doesn't mean something.”

sequence._describe: The crew and Ferret Tam discussing his ongoing safety and a new working arrangement, Marian Fletcher speaking with brisk practical focus. text: “What happens now,” Robin asked, once the two of them had rejoined the wider group, “with Crane, and everything else?”

“I stay put,” Tam said, after due consideration. “Moving again would only draw the kind of attention I've spent considerable effort avoiding. But I'll be a great deal more careful about who I deal with, and what I keep on hand, and I don't intend to give that agent — or his master — anything further to build a case from, real or imagined.”
“We'll help where we can,” Marian said. “Warning, mostly. If Crane's interest in you resurfaces, we'd rather you heard it from us before it became a second morning like the last one.”
“I'd take that gladly,” Tam said. “Consider it the first proper term of whatever arrangement we're building here.”

“Speaking of arrangements,” Marian continued, settling into the particular brisk practicality she brought to any genuinely useful negotiation, “we could use a man with your specific talents, going forward. Goods that need moving. Information that needs quiet channels. We've managed without a proper fence this long through luck and improvisation, mostly, and I'd rather not keep testing how long that luck holds.”

Tam considered this with real, careful attention — a man weighing an offer rather than simply accepting flattery. “I could manage that,” he said, finally. “Discreetly, and for fair terms on both sides. I'll admit the last few days have rather clarified for me which side of this arrangement I'd prefer to be standing on.”

text: They marked it properly that evening, back at camp, with considerably more food than the occasion strictly required and considerably more toasting than anyone present had any real talent for — Brother Crumb outdoing even his usual generous excess, Long John attempting a formal toast that dissolved, halfway through, into simple genuine warmth.

“To Ferret Tam,” Long John said, raising his cup, “who I have personally threatened, on Will's behalf, on at least two separate occasions, and who has nonetheless agreed to work with the lot of us regardless. That takes either remarkable forgiveness or a considerable lack of judgment, and I find I don't much care which.”
“Both, probably,” Tam said, raising his own cup in return. “I've made peace with that about myself some years back.”
“To debts properly settled,” Will added, quieter, raising his own cup with real feeling behind the words, “and to the people patient enough to let a man take his time settling them.”

“To that,” the whole gathered group agreed, and if Marian's eyes lingered a moment on Will during the toast — warm, considering, entirely unhurried — nobody present remarked on it, though more than one of them privately filed the moment away for later, entirely unbidden.

Grimalkin, from his usual perch, watched the whole proceeding with dry, characteristic amusement. “They're celebrating a man agreeing to be useful to them,” he observed to Barley. “Humans do love making an occasion of the obvious.”
“I love occasions,” Barley said, already angling hopefully toward the food. “Any occasion. All of them, really.”

sequence._describe: Robin of Loxby and Marian Fletcher sitting together by the fire in quiet conversation as the evening winds down, warm contemplative closing mood. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. Wide shot, 3:2 landscape aspect ratio, soft dying firelight, warm reflective mood.

text: The evening wound down slowly, warmly, the particular satisfied quiet of people who had settled something genuinely difficult and were permitting themselves, for one night at least, the simple pleasure of not immediately worrying about what came next.

“He'll do well by us,” Robin said, to Marian, watching Tam laugh at something Crumb had said, already thoroughly folded into the evening's warmth as though he'd always belonged there. “I rather think we'll do well by him too, for that matter.”

“I think so,” Marian agreed. “Though I'd not get too comfortable. Crane's patience hasn't gone anywhere simply because we survived one search of it. Whatever peace we've bought ourselves tonight, it's borrowed time, same as most of what we've managed to hold onto this past year.”
“Borrowed time's rather all we've ever had, though, isn't it,” Robin said, “if you look at it plainly. We've simply gotten better at spending it properly.”

Marian looked at him for a long moment — something warm and considering in her expression that had nothing to do with debts or investigations or anything else pressing on the evening — and allowed herself, for once, to simply agree without complicating it further.
“Yes,” she said. “I suppose we have.”

Behind them, the fire burned on, and the camp's laughter carried a while longer into the settling dark — one debt properly closed, one alliance properly begun, and considerably more waiting, patiently, just beyond the edges of tonight's hard-earned peace.
